newsitem.title: UK: Economists brush aside UK Labour's monetary plans.
newsitem.headline: Economists brush aside UK Labour's monetary plans.

text.p: Opposition Labour Party plans for Britain's monetary policy framework may be a small step forward, economists say, but they fall way short of what the financial markets really want -- an independent Bank of England.

On Wednesday, Labour's finance spokesman Gordon Brown said he would replace monthly meetings between the Chancellor of the Exchequer and Bank of England governor with a monetary panel made up of Bank representatives and three or four outsiders.

That would lower the risk of meetings becoming too personalised as well as limiting the chances of interest rates being set for political ends, Brown said. "So what?", replied a chorus of City economists.
"According to Mr. Brown this will depoliticise policy and make it free of short-term considerations," said David Coleman, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy. "Who is he kidding?"

He said the plans were no more than a trumped-up version of the present structure, popularly called the "Ken and Eddie show". While the Chancellor has the final say on interest rates, there will always be scope for political manipulation of monetary policy, he said.

Simon Briscoe, economist at Nikko Europe, said the one-on-one debates between Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke and Bank of England Governor Eddie George, far from being a weakness, were one of the system's great pluses.

"We now have an open and generally constructive debate about policy, and the current framework has enabled that," he said. "We believe the creative tension between Chancellor and Governor is a great strength."
Brown will finalise his plans after discussions with the Bank and with a new Council of Economic Advisers within the Treasury. But crucially, he will stop short of making the Bank independent.
The new council of advisers will replace Chancellor Kenneth Clarke's panel of independent advisers, known as the "wise persons." That idea also left Coleman cold.

Brown told BBC radio he would only consider an independent central bank when a structure had been properly evaluated and the advice given by the monetary panel had a track record. "I will look at the situation after we evaluate those two things."
Brown has accused Clarke of keeping base rates on hold at six percent because elections are due by May, rather than for economic reasons.
The Labour Party, standing up to 20 points ahead in the polls, is hotly tipped to win the next election.
But with the pound soaring and hitting exporters, and headline inflation running at just 2.8 percent year-on-year, the economic case for rate rises is far from cut and dried.
Whether a rate rise is needed now or not, Kate Barker, chief economist of top employers group the Confederation of British Industry, said the CBI favoured an independent Bank.
"In the longer run, we would prefer to see the Bank independent in day to day and month to month decisions, taking those decisions right out of the political arena," she said.

Barker, who also sits on the panel of independent advisers threatened with the axe by Brown, defended it. Because all of the members had full-time jobs elsewhere they had no "financial allegiance" to the system, she said. Briscoe, who does not favour an independent Bank, said there was room for improvement nonetheless. The Bank should focus more on the current trend and less on a target, currently 2.5 percent for underlying inflation, two years hence.

And it should have a wider remit, allowing it to comment on fiscal as well as monetary policy, he said. The role of the Treasury Select Committee -- a group of politicians briefed to monitor the economy -- could also be enhanced.

Brown's plans do not mention that. "We hope it is kite flying and the proposals will be watered down when Labour comes to power," Briscoe said. "Policy credibility is now growing and it is a bad time to tamper with it."
